newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa ship site of ice-breaking Zaire talks.
newsitem.headline: South Africa ship site of ice-breaking Zaire talks.

text.p: Russia built the SAS Outeniqua as an Arctic workhorse, but the ship dubbed "The Grey Diplomat" is now the best South Africa has to offer for an ice-breaking meeting between Zaire's warring rivals.

South African President Nelson Mandela, Deputy President Thabo Mbeki and U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun were to host a meeting on Friday aboard the ship between Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
The unarmed single-engined icebreaker then named Juvent, made obsolete by Russian budget cuts, became South Africa's first major military purchase in decades in 1993.
It now carries two 20mm anti-aircraft guns and a pair of Puma helicopters that operate from a pad overhanging the stern.
South Africa paid $12.8 million for the two-year-old vessel and has kept it hard at work as a naval supply ship, Antarctic support vessel and roving ambassador for African democracy.
"It's no luxury liner, but it's not at all bad for a naval vessel," said Jane's Defence Weekly correspondent Helmut Romer-Heitman.
The Outeniqua is named for a mountain range that runs along the Indian Ocean coastline. With its towering accommodation section perched in the bows, it is the navy's biggest ship.
In 1993 it delivered a mobile field hospital donated by South Africa's Moslem community to Bosnian Moslems.
The ship has carried medical supplies to the Indian Ocean islands of Madagascar and the Comoros.
In February 1995, the Outeniqua helped ferry 2,000 former political prisoners to Robben Island to mark the fifth anniversary of Mandela's release from jail.

Though built to the spartan standards of Russia's navy, the vessel has two comfortable suites on either side of the superstructure and a few comfortable cabins which officers are likely to give up to the delegates and diplomats.

The ship has a hospital, gym and indoor swimming pool and normally has a crew of 126. Converted cargo containers in the low mid-section serve as extra accommodation for the soldiers and scientists it sometimes carries.
Journalists seeking to cover the talks were warned that they might have to remain on the open deck through the day and that there would be nowhere for them to sleep.
